## God Kept the Promise Himself: The Son of David, the Son of Abraham (Matthew 1–2)
*How a genealogy of sinners and a virgin's child answer four hundred years of silence*

**Text:** Matthew 1–2 · **Supporting:** Genesis 12:1–3 · 2 Samuel 7:12–13 · Isaiah 7:14 · Micah 5:2 · Jeremiah 31:15 · Galatians 4:4

Most people who are done with the church did not leave over an argument. They left over a silence. They prayed, and heaven did not answer, and after enough of that a person quietly stops asking. Four hundred years is a long time to pray into a room that does not answer. That is the room Matthew opens in — Israel under Rome, the last prophet centuries dead, the old promises to Abraham and David sounding, by then, like the sort of thing an old man tells you before you learn how the world actually works. And into that silence Matthew does not open with a miracle or a voice from the sky. He opens with a list of names. A genealogy — the passage every reader has skipped. That is where the answer starts. Not with a feeling. With a record of fidelity that runs a thousand years deep.

### I. A Genealogy of Sinners: God Keeps His Word Through People Who Broke Theirs (Matthew 1:1–17)

Nobody starts a book this way. Forty-two generations, most of them names you cannot pronounce, and it reads like a legal document. But Matthew is not filling space; he is building a case, and the first verse is the thesis of the entire Gospel. "The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the Son of David, the Son of Abraham." (Matthew 1:1) The word Matthew uses is biblos geneseōs — the book of genesis, of origin, the same phrase that opens the Greek translation of Genesis itself. He is announcing a new creation, and he is doing it by naming two men. Abraham, who received the promise that in his offspring all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). David, who was told his son would sit on a throne established forever (2 Samuel 7:13). Every name between those two is a link in a chain God swore to hold across a thousand years and never let break.

- **A. The chain runs through failures, not saints.** Watch who Matthew puts in the line of the King. Judah, who slept with his daughter-in-law thinking she was a prostitute. Rahab, who was one. Manasseh, who filled Jerusalem with innocent blood. And David — named here not as the shepherd-poet but with the wound written in: "David the king begot Solomon by her who had been the wife of Uriah." (Matthew 1:6) Matthew will not even write Bathsheba's name. He writes the crime instead. Adultery. A murdered husband. The King's line runs straight through the King's worst sin, and Matthew refuses to sand it smooth. This is not a family cleaning up its history for the record. This is a God who keeps promises through people who kept nothing.
- **B. The women are the tell.** Ancient genealogies did not list women, and when Matthew breaks that rule he breaks it four times before Mary — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and "the wife of Uriah." Three of the four are foreigners: a Canaanite, a Moabite, a woman whose marriage was a scandal. The blessing promised to Abraham was for all the nations of the earth, and Matthew is quietly proving God had been keeping it for generations already, through the outsiders and the shamed, long before the King arrived. The mercy was in the machinery the whole time. We read our own lineage of failure — the addictions, the divorces, the fathers who left — and assume it disqualifies us from anything God would build. Matthew is telling us that God has been writing salvation through exactly that kind of line since the beginning. The scandal is not a threat to the promise. The scandal is where the promise runs.

### II. A Virgin's Son Named for What He Came to Do (Matthew 1:18–2:23)

Then the chain does something a chain cannot do. Forty times Matthew has written the word "begot" — this man fathered that one, the ordinary way the world makes more of itself. And then, at Joseph, the pattern breaks. Not "Joseph begot Jesus." Joseph is "the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus." (Matthew 1:16) The Greek shifts to a passive verb — of whom Jesus was born — because the acting agent is no longer a man. The line reaches its end, human effort runs out, and God reaches in. Isaiah had said it seven centuries before, in the reign of Ahaz around 735 BC, to a faithless king who would not even ask for a sign: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a Son, and shall call His name Immanuel." (Isaiah 7:14) Matthew quotes it and then glosses it for anyone who might miss the weight — "God with us." That is the whole point. Not a prophet about God. Not a message from God. God, with us, in a body, in a feed trough, in a nation He would have been within His rights to abandon.

- **A. The name is a job, not a sentiment.** The angel does not tell Joseph to name the child something noble or hopeful. "You shall call His name JESUS, for He will save His people from their sins." (Matthew 1:21) Yeshua — Yahweh saves. The name is not an aspiration pinned on the child; it is the child's assignment, written into Him before He draws a breath. And notice what He saves them from. Not from Rome. Not from poverty. Not from Herod. From their sins — the thing under every other thing, the deeper occupation that four hundred years of silence had finally exposed. The nation was waiting for rescue from Caesar. God sent rescue from the estrangement that no political change could touch. Every messiah the people had ever wanted would have taken the throne and left the heart untouched. This one was named, before birth, for the wound no throne could reach. Joseph is asked to speak the whole gospel every time he calls the boy in from the yard for supper.
- **B. The prophecies converge, and the violence comes with them.** Micah had named the town seven centuries early — Bethlehem, "though you are little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of you shall come forth to Me the One to be Ruler in Israel" (Micah 5:2) — and the King is born there, exactly. But read what surrounds the manger. Herod, an old man terrified of a rival throne, orders every boy under two in Bethlehem killed, and Matthew reaches back for Jeremiah: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, refusing to be comforted, because they are no more." (Jeremiah 31:15) The King comes, and blood follows Him from the first week. The Gospel that opens with a promise kept does not pretend the world lays out a welcome. It records the mothers of Bethlehem. It keeps their grief in the story, unresolved, right beside the good news. A God who came into a world like this did not come at a safe distance.

### III. The God Who Would Not Send a Substitute — Living Well When Heaven Seems Silent

Here is where it turns onto us. We have wanted, most of us, a God who sends help. A word, a sign, a better circumstance, a plan we can execute — help from a safe distance, the way you wire money to a crisis you have no intention of entering. And the church has often been glad to sell us that God: principles, techniques, a life-improvement scheme with Jesus somewhere in the branding, a deity who will manage your situation without ever coming into your actual room. I have preached that God myself, on a Sunday when it was easier to hand people a takeaway than to hand them Immanuel. It is the oldest counterfeit there is — a God who fixes your circumstances from orbit and never has to touch the mess.

- **A. The cost was His, not a delegate's.** In the fourth century the church came to the edge of losing exactly this, and Athanasius, a young deacon from Alexandria, spent his life fighting for it. Against those who wanted a lesser Christ — a created being, a spiritual intermediary, God's errand-boy — Athanasius argued that only God could save us and only a man needed saving, so the Savior had to be both, fully God with us in the flesh, or there was no salvation at all. The Council of Nicaea in AD 325 wrote it into the creed against every religious instinct to keep the deity at arm's length. That fight was not academic hairsplitting. If God sent a substitute, then in your worst hour you are being handled from a distance by a God who would not come down into it. Matthew's genealogy of sinners and Matthew's virgin-born Son are one long answer to that fear. He came Himself. Into the failure. Into the shame. Into Bethlehem while Herod sharpened the knife.
- **B. The silence was never absence.** Those four hundred years between the last prophet and the first Christmas felt, to everyone living through them, like abandonment. They were gestation. God was keeping His promise the entire time — through Tamar and Rahab and a compromised king and a string of names you were tempted to skip — arranging every link so that when the moment came, "when the fullness of the time had come, God sent forth His Son, born of a woman" (Galatians 4:4). Paul's phrase is exact: the fullness of the time. Not a delay God finally got around to ending. A appointed hour He was moving toward the whole while, through the very years that looked to everyone inside them like nothing. What you are calling His silence in your own life may be that same faithfulness working underground, in the part of the story you cannot read yet, in the stretch that feels like nothing is happening and no one is listening. That is not a comfort that lifts the weight off you. It is a harder claim, and a heavier one: that you are being asked to trust the God who came all the way down for the grieving mothers of Bethlehem, who did not spare Himself the manger or the flight to Egypt or the knife, and who has never once mistaken His silence for His absence, even when you have.

The name says everything the genealogy was building toward. He will save His people from their sins — not from a distance, not by proxy, not with advice slipped under the door. He came into the line of failures, wore our flesh, and took the name that means the whole rescue. You have been waiting, maybe for years, for God to send something into the silence. Read the first two chapters of Matthew again. He already sent Himself.

God kept the promise himself.

## Where Israel Fell, the Son Stood: The Beloved Son Tested in the Wilderness (Matthew 3–4:11)
*What the baptism and the temptation reveal about the obedience your salvation is built on*

**Text:** Matthew 3–4:11 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 8:2–3 · Exodus 4:22–23 · Isaiah 42:1 · Hosea 11:1 · Hebrews 4:15 · Romans 5:19

There is a version of Christianity that treats Jesus mainly as an example — a good man, a wise teacher, the model of the life you are supposed to be living. And there is a real hunger in the post-Christian world for exactly that Jesus, because a moral example makes no claim on you that you cannot quietly renegotiate. You admire it, you fall short of it, you feel a manageable guilt, and you move on with your week. What Matthew shows us in the wilderness is something the example-only reading cannot survive. Jesus does not go into that desert to demonstrate a technique for you. He goes in as your representative, to win the war you have already lost, at the exact three points where you keep losing it.

### I. The Voice at the Jordan Names Him Before He Has Done Anything (Matthew 3:1–17)

John the Baptist has been out at the Jordan in camel's hair, eating locusts, preaching the one line the comfortable never want to hear: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." (Matthew 3:2) He is the last of the prophets, the voice Isaiah foretold crying in the wilderness, and he is not gentle with the religious crowd — "Brood of vipers," he calls the Pharisees and Sadducees who come out to watch the spectacle, warning them not to lean on their pedigree, "We have Abraham as our father." Then Jesus arrives to be baptized, and John recoils, because this is backward. The sinless one submitting to a baptism of repentance He does not need. Jesus answers, "Permit it to be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness." (Matthew 3:15) He is stepping down into that water not because He needs to repent, but because from the very first act of His ministry He is standing in the place of the people who do.

- **A. The Father speaks first, before the work begins.** As Jesus comes up out of the water, the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice comes from heaven: "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." (Matthew 3:17) Notice the timing, because everything depends on it. No miracles yet. No Sermon on the Mount, no cross, no empty tomb. The Father's declared pleasure lands before the ministry has produced a single thing. The word beloved — agapētos — and the announcement of pleasure arrive as pure gift, not as wage. The Son is loved before He performs. Everything He does afterward flows out of an identity He is given at the river, not one He has to construct through achievement. We have that order exactly reversed in our own lives, and the reversal is quietly killing us — we perform in order to earn a verdict that, for Him, came first and free.
- **B. The whole Trinity stands at the river.** Father speaking from heaven, Son standing in the water, Spirit descending between them — Matthew shows you all three at once, and he does it in the language of Isaiah's servant song. "Behold! My Servant whom I uphold, My Elect One in whom My soul delights! I have put My Spirit upon Him." (Isaiah 42:1) The King is being publicly installed and the Servant is being commissioned in the same moment, and the two callings are the same calling. The one the Father delights in is the one who will be despised and rejected; the beloved Son is the suffering Servant; there is no other Christ hiding behind this one. But watch where the coronation leads. The Spirit that descends as a dove immediately drives Him — Mark's word is even harsher, ekballō, thrown out — into the desert to be tested. The same Spirit that anointed Him at the river hands Him over to the wilderness. The same beloved Son. The pleasure of God leading not to a throne and a crown but to forty days of hunger and a face-to-face confrontation with the enemy. This is the pattern of the whole Christian life in miniature: the word of the Father's love comes first, and then, not instead of it but because of it, the testing comes.

### II. Forty Days Against Forty Years: The Son Succeeds Where the Nation Failed (Matthew 4:1–11)

You cannot read the temptation rightly without reading Deuteronomy underneath it, because Jesus cannot. Israel was God's son — "Israel is My son, My firstborn," God told Pharaoh through Moses (Exodus 4:22) — and that son was led out into the wilderness for forty years to be tested, God says, "to humble you and test you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep His commandments or not." (Deuteronomy 8:2) They failed the test at every point. They grumbled for bread. They demanded that God prove Himself. They bowed to a golden calf. Now the true Son, the beloved firstborn Matthew has just shown us at the Jordan, is led into the same wilderness — forty days for their forty years — and tested at the exact three points where the nation collapsed. And He answers each temptation with a verse from Deuteronomy 6 through 8, from the very sermon Moses preached about that failure in the desert.

- **A. Bread, sign, and worship — the three ancient failures, reversed.** "If You are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread," the tempter says to a man who has not eaten in forty days, and Jesus answers, "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God." (Matthew 4:4, quoting Deuteronomy 8:3) Where Israel grumbled and doubted God's provision, the Son trusts the Father in the hunger. Then, throw Yourself from the temple and make God catch You — where Israel tested God at Massah, demanding He prove Himself, the Son refuses: "You shall not tempt the LORD your God." Then, all the kingdoms of the world, if You will fall down and worship me — where Israel bowed to the calf while Moses was still on the mountain, the Son will not bend: "You shall worship the LORD your God, and Him only you shall serve." (Matthew 4:10) Three temptations. Three ancient national failures. Three faithful answers, in order.
- **B. He fought with Scripture and obedience, not raw power.** This is the detail that proves He is standing in for us and not merely showing off. He does not vaporize the tempter with a word or summon legions of angels, though He could. He does the ordinary, unglamorous thing that a faithful son of Israel was always supposed to do and never did — He takes God at His word and obeys, verse by verse, in the weakness of a starved body. Hebrews says it without flinching: He "was in all points tempted as we are, yet without sin." (Hebrews 4:15) The victory is real precisely because the temptation was real. The hunger was real. The offer of every kingdom without the agony of the cross was a real offer, and it was aimed at the deepest want. And He stood. Not from a position of ease, but from inside the exact pressure that flattens us.

### III. The Obedience You Cannot Produce — Living Well When You Keep Failing the Test

Here is the turn, and it lands on us. We treat the Christian life as a wilderness we are supposed to conquer by trying harder — a series of tests we pass by sheer willpower, and every failure becomes one more count in the case we are quietly building against ourselves. That is Israel's story, and it is ours, and it ends the same way every single time: back in the desert, grumbling, bowing to whatever bread the tempter is offering this year. I have stood in a pulpit and preached "resist temptation, be stronger, want it more" as though the resisting were itself the gospel, and I have sent people home to a wilderness they were guaranteed to lose in, dressed a crushing burden up as encouragement, and called it a sermon.

- **A. His obedience is counted as yours.** The old theologians called this the active obedience of Christ — not only that He died for your sins, but that He kept the whole law you could never keep, and that flawless record is credited to everyone hidden in Him. Paul states it flatly: "For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so also by one Man's obedience many will be made righteous." (Romans 5:19) The first Adam failed his test in a garden with everything he needed. The last Adam passed His in a desert with nothing. When the Father looks at you now, the pleasure He declared over the beloved Son at the Jordan is the verdict spoken over everyone in Him. You do not enter the wilderness of your ordinary Tuesday in order to earn that verdict. You enter it already carrying it, which is the only reason you can face the temptation without your whole identity riding on the outcome.
- **B. Identity comes before the battle, or the battle destroys you.** Notice the order Matthew is so careful to keep. "This is My beloved Son" comes first, at the river; only then comes the desert. And the tempter's first two attacks begin with the same three words: "If You are the Son of God." He goes for the identity first, every time, because a person who is unsure whether they are loved will do almost anything to prove it — will turn stones to bread, will throw themselves off the temple, will bow to whoever promises to make the ache stop. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from a Nazi prison cell in 1944 while everything that could define a man was being stripped from him, kept circling the question "Who am I?" — the strong one others saw, or the trembling one he felt himself to be — and finally set the whole question down: "Whoever I am, Thou knowest, O God, I am Thine." That is the exact ground Jesus stood on in the wilderness, and it is the only ground that holds under you. You are not fighting your temptations in order to become beloved. You fight them because, in Christ, you already are.

The desert did not make Him the Son. It proved Him the Son — in your place, at every point you have caved — so that when you fall, and you will, the standing that was won there is already counted as yours. This is the difference between an example and a Savior, and it is the difference between exhaustion and rest. An example says: here is the life; go and match it. A Savior says: here is the life; I lived it in your place, and I give it to you. The example-Jesus leaves you alone in your own wilderness with a good model and a steadily worsening conscience, one more failure filed against you every week. The real Jesus went into the wilderness first, for you, against the very temptations that flatten you, and came out having won the war you keep losing — so that the fight left to you is no longer a fight for your identity, but a fight from one already secured at a river you did not stand beside.

Where Israel fell, the Son stood.

## The Kingdom Begins in the Heart: The Kingdom and Its Righteousness (Matthew 4:12–7:12)
*Why a righteousness that exceeds the Pharisees cannot be produced by rule-keeping*

**Text:** Matthew 4:12–7:12 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 9:1–2 · Jeremiah 31:33 · Ezekiel 36:26 · Psalm 51:6 · Micah 6:8 · Romans 3:20

We are living through the largest experiment in self-improvement in human history, and it is producing exhausted people. The whole culture runs on one promise: that if you get the external behaviors right — the habits, the routines, the metrics, the optimized morning, the curated self — the inner life will eventually fall into line behind them. Manage the outside and the inside will follow. It is the oldest religion there is, and it has a name in Matthew: the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees. And Jesus climbs a mountain, sits down in front of a crowd of tired people, and tells them that this righteousness — the most disciplined moral machinery the ancient world had ever produced — is not enough to get a single person through the door of the kingdom. He is not raising the bar higher. He is telling them the bar was never on the outside at all.

### I. The King Announces a Kingdom and Calls It Blessed to Be Empty-Handed (Matthew 4:12–5:12)

Jesus withdraws to Galilee, to the region Isaiah had called "Galilee of the Gentiles," the backwater where "the people who sat in darkness have seen a great light" (Isaiah 9:1–2). And His first sermon is exactly one line, the same line the Baptist preached: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." (Matthew 4:17) The verb — metanoeō — is not "feel bad." It is turn the whole mind and life around. Then He calls fishermen off their boats — Peter, Andrew, James, John — and they leave the nets, which is the entire point of the scene: the kingdom comes as a call to follow a person, not a program to adopt in your spare time. Then He goes up on the mountain, sits down in the posture of a rabbi teaching with authority, and opens with the Beatitudes — nine pronouncements of blessing that describe a kind of person the world would never call blessed.

- **A. Blessed are the ones with nothing to offer.** Read carefully who Jesus calls blessed — makarios, a deep and settled flourishing that does not rise and fall with your circumstances. "Blessed are the poor in spirit." "Blessed are those who mourn." "Blessed are the meek." "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness." (Matthew 5:3–6) Every one of these is a description of spiritual bankruptcy — people who know they have nothing to bring, who grieve their own condition instead of managing it, who are starving for a rightness they cannot manufacture no matter how hard they work at it. The kingdom does not begin with the accomplished, the disciplined, or the impressive. It begins with the empty. The Pharisee, full of his own record and proud of it, is the one standing furthest from the door precisely because he cannot imagine needing it opened for him.
- **B. The blessing is not a reward for a new posture.** Do not misread the Beatitudes as a fresh list of virtues to perform — "be poorer in spirit, mourn a little harder, work up some meekness." That would collapse the whole sermon back into the Pharisee's project of self-manufacture. The Beatitudes describe what the King's grace produces in a person, not what a person produces to purchase the King. They are the shape a heart takes once it has finally stopped pretending it has things under control. And they end, tellingly, with persecution — "Blessed are you when they revile and persecute you and say all kinds of evil against you falsely for My sake" (Matthew 5:11) — because this kind of life does not flatter the world, and the world can feel that it is not being flattered. The blessed life is not the comfortable one. It is the one that has quit performing for an audience.

### II. A Righteousness That Exceeds the Pharisees Comes From a Remade Heart (Matthew 5:17–6:18)

Then Jesus says the line that reframes everything that follows: "unless your righteousness exceeds the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven." (Matthew 5:20) The crowd would have heard that as flatly impossible — the Pharisees were the gold standard of external obedience, tithing the herbs on their spice racks, fasting twice a week, building fences around the law so they would never even come near breaking it. How does an ordinary Galilean fisherman exceed that? Jesus answers with a series of six statements, each shaped the same way: "You have heard that it was said... but I say to you." And every one of them drives the commandment off the surface of behavior and down into the interior of the heart, where the Pharisee's machinery could never reach.

- **A. He moves the commandment inside the chest.** You have heard "you shall not murder" — but I say the settled anger and the contempt in your chest is already the thing the commandment was after. You have heard "you shall not commit adultery" — but I say the look that lingers and cultivates has already committed it in the heart. (Matthew 5:21–28) He is not adding new external rules to the old ones. He is exposing that the law was always aimed at the heart, and that the Pharisee's spotless hands were hiding a filthy interior he had learned not to examine. The prophets had said this the entire time. God "desires truth in the inward parts" (Psalm 51:6), David confessed after his own external religion failed to keep him from Bathsheba. Micah asked what the Lord actually requires and answered not with more sacrifices but "to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:8). External religion was always, at bottom, a way of managing God without ever surrendering the one thing He was after.
- **B. The remedy is not more effort but a new interior.** If the real problem is the heart, then no amount of behavior modification can reach it — "by the deeds of the law no flesh will be justified in His sight" (Romans 3:20). You cannot scrub an inside clean by polishing an outside. But this is precisely what the prophets promised the new covenant would finally accomplish. Jeremiah, promising the covenant that would replace the broken one: "I will put My law in their minds, and write it on their hearts." (Jeremiah 31:33) Ezekiel, promising it in even sharper terms: "I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will take the heart of stone out of your flesh and give you a heart of flesh." (Ezekiel 36:26) The righteousness that exceeds the Pharisees is not a stricter, more heroic compliance. It is a transplant. It is the kingdom itself taking up residence in a place no rule could ever get to, doing surgery no discipline could perform.

### III. The One Thing You Cannot Optimize — Living Well When the Outside Is Clean and the Inside Is Not

Here is the mirror, and it is aimed at us. We have built an entire civilization of Pharisees who would be genuinely horrified to be called religious. We track our steps and our sleep and our productivity and our moral brands, the whole apparatus of a self kept presentable on the surface for an audience we are always half-aware of. And the church has too often baptized the whole thing, selling Jesus as the best life-improvement plan on the market — the missing habit, the final upgrade that at last makes the optimization system deliver. I have done it. I have handed people five clean steps from a stage and called it a sermon, managed their behavior for forty minutes and never once laid a finger on their hearts, because the heart is the one thing I cannot optimize and therefore, if I am honest, the one thing I was most tempted to leave completely alone.

- **A. The Pharisee is not out there; he is in here.** In the late fourth century, Augustine — who had spent years carefully managing his public reputation as a brilliant rising rhetorician while his interior life was quietly coming apart — wrote in his Confessions that he had loved his own sin and loved the approval of other men more than he loved God, and that no external reform, no philosophy, no strategy of self-discipline had ever touched it, until grace reached the will itself and remade the wanting. He is describing, from the inside, the exact problem Jesus names on the mountain. The scribe and the Pharisee are not a first-century sect we get to look down on from a safe distance. They are the human factory setting — the deep impulse to keep the outside presentable so that no one, including God, ever gets access to the inside. Turn around. The clean surface is the disguise, and I have worn it in a robe, on a platform, with a Bible open in my hands.
- **B. Christ produces what He commands.** This is finally why the Sermon on the Mount is not a crushing new to-do list but the portrait of a life the King Himself creates in a person. He is the poor-in-spirit one who wept over Jerusalem, the meek one who did not break the bruised reed, the pure in heart, the merciful, the peacemaker, the persecuted righteous one who was reviled and did not revile back — the Sermon on the Mount is, before it is anything else, a portrait of the One preaching it. And by His Spirit He writes that same heart into the people who follow Him, slowly, from the inside out, until the character described on the mountain is the character being formed in the pew. You do not climb the mountain in order to earn your way into the kingdom by out-Phariseeing the Pharisees. The King came down the mountain, went to a cross, and sent a Spirit to give you the heart of flesh you could never grow on your own by any effort. Even the command that seems most impossible — "be perfect, as your Father in heaven is perfect" (Matthew 5:48) — is not a whip laid across your back. It is a promise about where grace has decided to take you.

You cannot manage your way into the kingdom of heaven. You can only be remade into it, from the inside, by a hand that is not your own. The King is not asking for a cleaner outside from you. He is after the one thing you have spent your whole life guarding, decorating, and keeping just out of everyone's reach — including His.

The kingdom begins in the heart.

## Hearing Is Not Yet Obeying: Two Roads, Two Builders, One Authority (Matthew 7:13–7:29)
*Why the danger at the end of the Sermon on the Mount is not the pagan but the admirer*

**Text:** Matthew 7:13–29 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 30:19 · Jeremiah 17:9 · Ezekiel 33:31–32 · James 1:22–24 · Luke 6:46 · 1 John 2:4

There is a way of relating to Jesus that feels exactly like faith and is not. You listen. You are moved. You would say, if anyone asked, that you agree with Him, admire Him, are genuinely drawn to His teaching. And then you go home, and nothing in the way you actually live your Monday has been forced to change by any of it. Jesus ends the greatest sermon ever preached by aiming everything — the whole weight of the mountain — at exactly that person. Not the skeptic who rejects Him outright, but the crowd that nods along and goes home unchanged. He closes with four hard either-ors, and every one of them refuses to let the admirer stay a comfortable admirer for one more minute.

### I. Two Gates, Two Trees, Two Confessions — The Sermon Ends in a Fork (Matthew 7:13–23)

The whole Sermon on the Mount has been building a portrait of the kingdom heart, and now Jesus makes the crowd stand at a fork and choose a road. "Enter by the narrow gate; for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and there are many who go in by it." (Matthew 7:13) This is the ancient covenant choice Moses set before Israel on the plains of Moab — "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing; therefore choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19) — but now pressed down to a single sharp point. Two gates. Two roads. Two destinations, and no third option quietly available in the middle. And the tell, the thing that should stop us, is that the road to destruction is the crowded one. Numbers are not evidence of being right. The majority is on the wide road, and they are comfortable there precisely because they have so much company.

- **A. Fruit exposes the tree over time.** Jesus warns next of false prophets who come "in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves," and He gives the one reliable test: "You will know them by their fruits." (Matthew 7:16) A good tree cannot produce bad fruit, and a bad tree cannot produce good; the life eventually reveals the root, whatever the presentation claims. This is not a commission to become a suspicious fruit-inspector of everyone else in the pew. It is a sober warning that religious presentation is never itself proof of a good tree — the wolf can wear the wool convincingly for years. What a life actually produces, over the long run and under pressure, tells the truth that the profession by itself never can.
- **B. The most terrifying words in the Gospel.** Then Jesus says the thing that should stop every religious person cold. "Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord,' shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of My Father in heaven." (Matthew 7:21) There will be people on the last day who called Him Lord, who prophesied in His name, cast out demons in His name, did many wonders in His name — and He will say to them, "I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness." (Matthew 7:23) Read the verb carefully. Not "I knew you and then lost you." I never knew you. The religious activity was real, undeniable, even impressive — and the relationship underneath it was never there at all. Jesus is not warning the irreligious in this passage. He is warning the busy, confessing, ministry-doing, Lord-saying crowd. Saying "Lord" is not the same thing as knowing the Lord, and a person can say it for a lifetime and still hear those words at the end.

### II. Two Builders and the Storm That Tests Every Foundation (Matthew 7:24–27)

Jesus lands the entire sermon on one image, and the image is a decision no one in the crowd can avoid making. "Therefore whoever hears these sayings of Mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock." (Matthew 7:24) And the other man — the fool — hears the very same sayings and does not do them, and builds his house on sand. Notice everything that is identical between the two men, because the identical parts are the whole warning. Both of them hear the sermon. Both of them build a house. Both houses stand up perfectly fine in good weather. The single difference between the wise man and the fool, the only variable in the entire parable, is doing.

- **A. The storm reveals what fair weather hides.** "And the rain descended, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it fell. And great was its fall." (Matthew 7:27) The two houses looked exactly alike right up until the storm arrived. Same neighborhood, same street, same appearance from the road — the only difference was underground, in the foundation, where no visitor could see it and where the builder himself could forget it was ever a question. This is why so many people discover the true state of their foundation only when everything is already coming apart — the marriage failing, the diagnosis, the funeral, the collapse they never planned for and cannot pray away. In the calm, a hearing-only faith and a hearing-and-doing faith are genuinely indistinguishable, even to the person living inside one, even to the pastor watching from the front. The storm is not the enemy of your faith. The storm is the honest test that finally tells you what you were actually standing on the whole time you assumed you already knew — and it is a mercy, however it feels, to find out while there is still time to dig down to rock.
- **B. Doing is the difference, and doing is exactly what we edit out.** James, who sat under this sermon as Jesus' own younger brother, later put it as plainly as it can be put: "But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves." (James 1:22) He compares the hearer-only to a man who looks intently at his face in a mirror and then walks away and immediately forgets what he looked like — the word had no purchase, changed nothing, left no mark. Ezekiel had named the ancient version of the same self-deception centuries before, describing a congregation that comes and sits and listens attentively, "and they hear your words, but they do not do them; for with their mouth they show much love, but their heart pursues their own gain. Indeed you are to them as a very lovely song of one who has a pleasant voice." (Ezekiel 33:31–32) A lovely song you enjoy and applaud and never once obey. That is the sand foundation, described by a prophet six hundred years early.

### III. The Peril of the Admirer — Living Well in a Culture That Loves Jesus and Ignores Him

Turn it around, because this is aimed squarely at the pews and not at the pagans outside. The gravest spiritual danger in a post-Christian culture is not open, articulate rejection — the honest atheist at least knows where he stands and has not deceived himself. It is warm, sincere, genuinely moved admiration that never once becomes obedience — the person who can quote the Sermon on the Mount, who reposts it, who finds Jesus beautiful and even weeps at the right lines, and who has quietly arranged an entire life around not doing a single word of what He actually said. The post-Christian West is full of Jesus-admirers who left the church and kept the sentiment, and full of church-attenders who never left the building and never obeyed a word inside it. Both are on the sand. Neither knows it, because the sand holds fine on a sunny day. And I am inside this indictment before I get to name anyone else. I have preached these very verses and then driven home from the church building having heard myself say things from the pulpit that I had no serious intention of doing on Monday morning. I have called Him "Lord, Lord" in front of a congregation. The warning in Matthew 7 has my name written into it before it has anyone else's.

- **A. Admiration is the counterfeit that fools the sincere.** In the 1840s, the Danish thinker Søren Kierkegaard drew the exact line that exposes us — the difference between an admirer of Christ and a follower of Christ. The admirer, he wrote, keeps himself carefully at a safe distance; he applauds the teaching, he is genuinely and even tearfully moved by it, and he takes great care that his own life is never actually claimed or rearranged by it. The follower, by contrast, does the costly thing the teaching requires and pays for it. And Kierkegaard's whole warning to his comfortable Christian society was that Christendom had quietly turned nearly the entire church into a vast congregation of admirers who had never once noticed that they were not, in fact, disciples of anyone. That is the sand foundation, described in a nineteenth-century Danish accent. The apostle John says it with no cushioning left on it at all: "He who says, 'I know Him,' and does not keep His commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him." (1 John 2:4)
- **B. The authority under the choice is the King Himself.** Matthew closes the whole sermon by telling us exactly how the crowd reacted: "the people were astonished at His teaching, for He taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes." (Matthew 7:28–29) The word is exousia — a real, inherent authority He simply possessed, not one borrowed from a chain of rabbinic tradition the way the scribes had to borrow theirs. This is what makes the two roads a genuine, weight-bearing fork and not a friendly suggestion you can take or leave. The One standing there saying "do them" is the King who will judge, the One who on the last day says either "I never knew you" or "well done, good and faithful servant." The obedience He calls for is not a frantic works-project to earn His favor. It is the only honest, coherent response there is to who He actually is. You cannot admire this King into His kingdom. The house on the rock is simply the life that finally does what it heard Him say.

The storm is coming for every house on both roads, the wise man's and the fool's alike. Jesus does not promise the doer a life without weather; He promises him a house that stands when the weather comes. That is the only thing the doing buys, and it is everything. The only question the Sermon on the Mount leaves you standing there holding is which foundation you have actually been building on all this time while the weather was still fair and everything looked fine from the road — and whether the Lord you keep addressing so warmly, so sincerely, so often, is a Lord you have ever, on a single ordinary Monday, when it cost you something and no one was watching, actually obeyed.

Hearing is not yet obeying.

## He Came for the Sick: Authority Over Everything That Breaks Us (Matthew 8–9)
*What ten miracles reveal about the kind of people the King actually came to save*

**Text:** Matthew 8–9 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 53:4 · Hosea 6:6 · Psalm 107:28–29 · Ezekiel 34:5–6 · Numbers 27:17 · Romans 5:8

Ask most people why they keep their distance from God, and underneath the intellectual reasons you will usually find one quiet conviction doing all the real work: that they are not the kind of person God is actually interested in. Too far gone. Too compromised. Too tired to start. Too much of a wreck to belong in a room full of people who seem to have it together. Church, they have concluded, is for the sorted-out, and they know for certain they are not. Matthew stacks up nine or ten miracles across two chapters — power over disease, demons, storms, paralysis, and death itself — and then, right in the middle of all that power, he tells you exactly who all of it is for. And it turns out to be precisely the people who had already counted themselves out.

### I. Authority Over Everything That Breaks a Body and a Life (Matthew 8:1–9:8)

Matthew has just shown us the King's words on the mountain; now he shows us the King's power down on the ground, and he arranges the miracles deliberately to demonstrate authority over every force that ruins a human life. A leper, ritually untouchable under the law, cut off from every human being — and Jesus does the one thing no one else would do: "Then Jesus put out His hand and touched him" (Matthew 8:3), and the man is clean. A Roman centurion's servant healed at a distance by nothing but a spoken word, and Jesus marvels aloud at a Gentile faith greater than any He has found in Israel. A storm on the Sea of Galilee violent enough to terrify seasoned fishermen, and Jesus stands up and rebukes the wind and the water and there is "a great calm" (Matthew 8:26) — doing the thing Psalm 107 says belongs to the LORD alone: "He calms the storm, so that its waves are still." A man tormented by demons, set free with a word. A paralytic lowered before Him and told, first of all, "Son, be of good cheer, your sins are forgiven you." (Matthew 9:2)

- **A. The healings are the bearing of our brokenness.** Matthew refuses to leave the miracles as bare displays of raw power. He stops and interprets them for us: Jesus healed the sick "that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaiah the prophet, saying: 'He Himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses.'" (Matthew 8:17, quoting Isaiah 53:4) The Servant of Isaiah 53 does not repair us from a safe distance. He takes it onto Himself, into Himself. Every healing in these two chapters is a preview of the cross, where the entire weight of a broken world — sickness, sin, death, all of it — would be lifted onto the one Man who came precisely to bear it. The power is never mere spectacle. It is the down payment on a substitution.
- **B. The paralytic exposes the real disease.** When they lower the paralyzed man through the crowd, Jesus' very first word to him is not "rise" but "your sins are forgiven you." The scribes are immediately scandalized — only God can forgive sins. Exactly right. That is the whole point He is making. And to prove He has the authority to do the invisible thing, He does the visible one on command: "Arise, take up your bed, and go to your house." (Matthew 9:6) The man walks out carrying the mat he was carried in on. And here is the thing we keep missing: the healing of the legs is the lesser of the two miracles, offered only as public evidence of the greater one already spoken. The King has authority over the thing that lies under every other thing. The broken body was never the deepest problem in that room, and it is not the deepest one in yours.

### II. The Physician Comes for the Sick, Not the Well (Matthew 9:9–13)

Then Matthew, with remarkable honesty, tells his own story, and it turns out to be the interpretive key to the entire section. Jesus is walking along and passes a tax booth — the single most despised job in all of Israel, a Jewish man collecting money for the Roman occupier, a traitor and a legalized thief by the very definition of the work — and He says two words to the man sitting there counting coins: "Follow Me." (Matthew 9:9) And Matthew gets up and follows Him. Then Matthew throws a party, and his house fills up with tax collectors and sinners, the moral wreckage of respectable Galilean society, all of them reclining at the table with Jesus in the middle of them, eating and talking and welcomed.

- **A. The objection and the verdict.** The Pharisees cannot stomach the scene: "Why does your Teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?" (Matthew 9:11) It is a completely fair question if you believe, as they sincerely did, that holiness means separation from the contaminated, that righteousness is a matter of who you refuse to touch. Jesus answers it with a single line that reorders everything: "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." (Matthew 9:12) A doctor is not defiled by walking into the room of the diseased; a doctor is defined by exactly that willingness to go where the sickness is. The scandal the Pharisees think they see is not an embarrassing exception to the mission. It is the mission, stated plainly at Matthew's own table. He did not come for the people who have it all together. There are none — but He especially did not come for the ones who are convinced that they do.
- **B. Mercy over sacrifice — the ancient word they had forgotten.** Then Jesus sends the experts back to their own Bibles with a stinging assignment: "But go and learn what this means: 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice.' For I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance." (Matthew 9:13, quoting Hosea 6:6) He is quoting the prophet Hosea against the professional keepers of sacrifice, telling the men who had built their whole identity on religious precision that they had never understood the God they claimed to serve. God has always wanted mercy more than machinery, the heart more than the ritual. And here is the terrible mechanism of it: the self-diagnosed righteous exclude themselves — not because grace was ever unavailable to them, but because you cannot receive a physician while you are still insisting, loudly, that you are perfectly well. The tax collectors got in through the one door the Pharisees had bolted shut from the inside. And the only key was the one thing the tax collectors had and the Pharisees refused to admit: they knew exactly what they were.

### III. Sheep Without a Shepherd — Living Well When You Have Decided You Are Too Far Gone

Turn it around onto us, because our version of the Pharisee's mistake is quieter than his and just as fatal. We have made the church, so often, a gathering for the already-sorted — the family with the marriage still visibly intact, the résumé of moral respectability, the person who would sooner die than let you see the actual wreckage in the basement. And so the genuinely sick stay home, certain they would be exposed and quietly disqualified, while the well congratulate one another on their good health and call it fellowship. I have helped build rooms exactly like that. I have preached in a way that made the put-together comfortable and the desperate invisible, and I did it while quoting, from that same platform, a Savior who reclined at dinner with sinners in a tax collector's living room.

- **A. The compassion that exposed a false comfort.** Matthew ends this whole section not on a note of triumph but on a note of grief. Jesus looks out at the crowds and "was moved with compassion for them, because they were weary and scattered, like sheep having no shepherd." (Matthew 9:36) The word is splanchnizomai — a gut-level, physical ache, compassion felt in the body. And He is deliberately quoting the prophets' old indictment of Israel's failed leaders. Ezekiel had thundered against the shepherds who fed only themselves while "My sheep were scattered over all the face of the earth, and no one was seeking or searching for them" (Ezekiel 34:5–6). The people were not scattered and weary because they were beyond all help. They were scattered because the very ones charged with shepherding them had abandoned the job to feed themselves. The tired and the far-gone are not God's rejects to be stepped over. They are His harvest, and He grieves — physically grieves — that no one has gone out to gather them in.
- **B. He proves the mercy at the cross, not merely at the clinic.** In the third and fourth centuries, when repeated plagues swept through the crowded cities of the Roman Empire, the historians record a striking pattern: the pagans fled their own dying, abandoning even close relatives in the street to die alone rather than risk infection, while the Christians stayed — nursing the sick, feeding the abandoned, burying the dead, and catching the disease themselves in the process. The emperor Julian, who despised the Christians and wanted to revive the old gods, complained bitterly in a letter that these "Galileans" cared for the sick even outside their own community and put the old religion to shame by it. That instinct did not come from nowhere. It came, in a straight line, from a Physician who touched the leper no one would touch, reclined with the traitor everyone despised, and finally proved the whole thing in the one place where words alone could never prove it: "But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." (Romans 5:8) Not once we were finally well. While we were still sick, still traitors, still at our worst — that is when He went to the cross.

You have believed a lie about yourself — that you are the exception, the one genuinely too broken for the door, the sickness too far along for this particular physician. So read the guest list at Matthew's table again. Read whose infirmities Isaiah says He bore. The one qualification the King is actually looking for turns out to be the very thing you have spent your whole life most ashamed of.

He came for the sick.

## Following Him Will Cost You: Sent as Sheep Among Wolves (Matthew 10)
*What the sending of the twelve reveals about the price of a discipleship the culture keeps trying to make painless*

**Text:** Matthew 10 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 2:3–6 · Micah 7:6 · John 15:20 · 2 Timothy 3:12 · Philippians 3:8 · Revelation 2:10

We have made following Jesus safe. Not in the sense of secure — in the sense of costless. The offer, as it usually reaches people now, is that Jesus will improve your life, calm your anxiety, bless your family, tidy up your marriage, and ask nothing back that would seriously disturb the shape of the life you already wanted. It is a warm, painless, thoroughly domesticated discipleship, and it sells. And then you open Matthew 10, where Jesus sends out the twelve on their first mission, and you find that almost the entire speech is a sustained warning about what following Him is going to cost them. He is not hiding the price to close the sale and spring it on them later. He is naming it out loud, up front, so that not one of them is ambushed when the bill comes due.

### I. The King Extends His Own Ministry Through Ordinary Men (Matthew 10:1–15)

Jesus calls the twelve to Himself and gives them "power over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal all kinds of sickness and all kinds of disease" (Matthew 10:1) — the very authority Matthew has just spent chapters 8 and 9 showing us at work in Jesus Himself. The mission is not something novel He is inventing for them; it is His own ministry extended outward through borrowed hands. He sends them first "to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" (Matthew 10:6), carrying the identical message He and John the Baptist had been preaching: "The kingdom of heaven is at hand." (Matthew 10:7) And He tells them to travel with almost nothing — no gold, no silver, no copper in their belts, no extra bag, no spare tunic, no staff beyond the one in their hand — because the worker is worthy of his food and the whole enterprise is designed to run on dependence, not on provisions carefully stockpiled in advance.

- **A. Freely you received, freely give.** "Freely you have received, freely give." (Matthew 10:8) The entire mission is grace flowing outward from men who paid nothing to receive it. They possess nothing that was not first handed to them, so they hand it on without price and without calculation. This one line is the death of the mercenary spirit before it can take a single breath — the moment ministry becomes a way to secure something for yourself, status or comfort or a living, it has already stopped being the mission Jesus actually sent. The twelve go out as men who own nothing, are owed nothing, and are guaranteed nothing, carrying in their empty hands a kingdom they did not build and cannot bill anyone for.
- **B. The message divides, and that division is not a failure.** Some houses will receive them and some will not. Where they are rejected, Jesus tells them to shake the very dust off their feet as they leave — the message itself sorts the ground it falls on, exactly as the sower's seed does. Jesus is deliberately preparing these men for the hard reality that faithful proclamation does not, and never did, guarantee acceptance. It guarantees a response, and the response is very often flat refusal. That refusal is not a sign that the workers did something wrong or failed to be winsome enough. It is precisely what every prophet before them met, all the way back to Ezekiel, sent to "a rebellious nation" and told plainly, "whether they hear or whether they refuse" (Ezekiel 2:3–5). The refusal was written into the job description from the beginning.

### II. Sheep Among Wolves: The Cost Named Plainly (Matthew 10:16–39)

Then the whole tone of the speech turns, and Jesus stops describing the mission and starts describing what the mission is going to do to the men carrying it. "Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves." (Matthew 10:16) Sit with the image, because He chose every word of it. Not sheep who quietly become wolves once they are out there. Not sheep issued fangs and claws for self-defense on the road. Sheep — defenseless, unarmed, easily killed — deliberately sent into the middle of predators, whose only protection in the entire world is the Shepherd who chose to send them there. He tells them plainly what to expect: they will be handed over to councils, flogged in the synagogues, dragged before governors and kings, and "you will be hated by all for My name's sake." (Matthew 10:22)

- **A. The cost reaches all the way into the family.** The sharpest cut in the whole speech is domestic, and Jesus does not soften it. Quoting Micah's picture of a whole society coming apart at the seams, He warns that "a man's enemies will be those of his own household" (Matthew 10:36, echoing Micah 7:6), and then He says the thing no one prints on a church sign or a coffee mug: "He who loves father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me. And he who loves son or daughter more than Me is not worthy of Me. And he who does not take his cross and follow after Me is not worthy of Me." (Matthew 10:37–38) Understand what the cross meant to the men hearing this. It was not a headache, an inconvenience, a hard season, or a difficult boss. To that audience the cross was a Roman execution device, a beam you carried on your own shoulders to the place where they would kill you on it. He is telling would-be followers, in the plainest terms available, that following Him may cost them the approval — and even the love — of the people they hold most dear, and that this is the actual price, not a metaphor for one.
- **B. A servant is not above his master.** He grounds every bit of the cost in Himself, so that no disciple can accuse Him of asking from a distance what He would not pay Himself. "A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master." (Matthew 10:24) If they called the master of the house Beelzebul — and they did — then His whole household will be slandered right along with Him. He is not asking His followers to walk into anything He will not walk into first, and worse. And then comes the paradox that reorders the entire arithmetic of a human life: "He who finds his life will lose it, and he who loses his life for My sake will find it." (Matthew 10:39) The self you clutch and protect at absolutely all costs is precisely the self you will forfeit in the end. The life you hand over to Him is the only one you actually get to keep. This is the exact calculation the domesticated, cost-free gospel is structurally unable to perform, because it was built from the ground up to promise you your life, not to ask for it.

### III. The Painless Discipleship That Cannot Save — Living Well When Faith Costs You Something Real

Turn it onto us now. We are the inheritors of a Christianity that has spent the better part of a century getting very good at removing the cost — at promising people all the benefits of Jesus while quietly deleting the sheep-among-wolves clause from the contract, so that when the cost finally does arrive, as Jesus promised it would, people naturally conclude they must have been sold a defective product and quietly return it. And I have done the deleting myself. I have preached the comfort and skipped the cross, offered people a Jesus carefully sized to fit inside the life they already had and did not want disturbed, because a costly gospel is harder to preach and much harder to hear, and, if I am honest, I wanted the room to stay full on Sunday.

- **A. Cheap grace against costly grace.** In 1937, in a Germany where the church had already made its peace with the regime, Dietrich Bonhoeffer named this exact thing with a precision no one has improved on since. He called it "cheap grace" — grace sold on the open market like cheapened goods, the preaching of forgiveness without requiring repentance, baptism without church discipline, communion without confession, grace without discipleship, grace without the cross. Cheap grace, he wrote, is the deadly enemy of the church, and we are fighting for our lives against it. Over against it he set costly grace: costly because it calls a man to follow, and costly because it costs a man his life; grace because it thereby gives him the only true life there is. Bonhoeffer was not writing theory in a comfortable study. He wrote it inside a church that had traded its soul for institutional safety, and eight years later, in April 1945, in the final weeks of the war, he was hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp for following to the end the Christ he had described on the page. He had learned the price of Matthew 10 by name and paid it. Paul, who paid it too, told Timothy the same thing without any softening: "Yes, and all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution." (2 Timothy 3:12) Not may. Will.
- **B. The one who counted everything loss and gained more.** But hear where the cost finally lands, because Jesus does not leave the twelve holding only an invoice. In the very same speech He tells them not to fear the ones who can only kill the body, that not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father's knowing, and that "the very hairs of your head are all numbered." (Matthew 10:30) The cost is entirely real, and the care over them is total, and both are true in the same breath, from the same mouth. And Paul, who paid the whole price to the very end and lost everything the world counts as gain, did the accounting himself and arrived at the only sane conclusion a man in his position could reach: "But indeed I also count all things loss for the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them as rubbish, that I may gain Christ." (Philippians 3:8) The one who loses his life for Christ finds it. That is not a slogan to hang on a wall. It is the settled testimony of every single person who has ever actually paid the price and found out, on the far side of it, what they got in return.

You have been offered, for most of your life, a Jesus who costs you nothing and asks nothing back. That Jesus does not exist. The real King sends sheep out among wolves, asks a man to carry his own cross, and warns you plainly right at the family dinner table — and He is worth every ounce of what He asks, precisely because the life you lose for His sake turns out to be the only life you were ever actually going to keep.

Following him will cost you.

## Come, All Who Are Weary: The Rejected King and the Unforgivable Hardness (Matthew 11–12)
*Why the kingdom is hidden from the confident and handed to the exhausted*

**Text:** Matthew 11–12 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 42:1–3 · Jeremiah 6:16 · Zechariah 7:11–12 · Proverbs 29:1 · Hebrews 3:15 · 1 Corinthians 1:27

There is a particular kind of tiredness the culture has no cure for. Not the ordinary tiredness a weekend or a vacation fixes — the deeper exhaustion of carrying yourself, of performing a self, of trying to be enough and never once arriving there. The tiredness of holding it all together for an audience that never leaves. And the strange thing about Matthew 11 and 12 is that this exhausted person is precisely the one Jesus turns and calls. Not the wise. Not the strong. Not the religious experts who had every conceivable advantage. The weary. These two chapters are one long, sustained study in rejection — John doubts Him, the cities refuse Him, the Pharisees blaspheme Him — and right in the dead center of all that hardening, Jesus opens His arms to the worn-out and simply says: come.

### I. The King Rejected by the Confident and the Comfortable (Matthew 11:1–24)

The rejection starts, painfully, with His own herald. John the Baptist, now locked in Herod's prison and awaiting execution, sends word through his disciples: "Are You the Coming One, or do we look for another?" (Matthew 11:3) The very man who baptized Him and pointed the crowds to Him is now doubting, because the King is not doing what John expected the King to do — no axe laid to the root of the trees, no winnowing fork, no unquenchable fire, just healing and quiet preaching while John himself rots in a cell for having told the truth. And Jesus does not rebuke the doubt. He sends back the evidence of Isaiah: "The blind see and the lame walk; the lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear; the dead are raised up and the poor have the gospel preached to them." (Matthew 11:5) The King is fulfilling Scripture to the letter — just not the version of it that anyone, even His own herald, had wanted.

- **A. The generation that refuses every tune.** Jesus names the crowd's real problem with surgical precision: they are like children sitting in the marketplace who will not play no matter what song is offered. John came neither eating nor drinking, an ascetic, and they said he had a demon; the Son of Man came eating and drinking, at Matthew's table with sinners, and they called Him "a glutton and a winebibber, a friend of tax collectors and sinners." (Matthew 11:18–19) The issue was never the messenger's style, and it never is. It was a heart that had already decided not to respond, and would find a reason to reject whatever came. No approach on earth would have satisfied them, because the refusal was upstream of the evidence.
- **B. Woe to the privileged towns.** Then come the woes, and they fall on the most surprising heads. Chorazin. Bethsaida. Capernaum — the very towns that had seen the most miracles, that had the closest, most sustained exposure to the King walking their own streets. And Jesus says that pagan Tyre and Sidon, even Sodom itself, would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes if they had seen what these Galilean towns saw and shrugged at. (Matthew 11:21–23) The greater the privilege, the greater the accountability — that is the sobering law running underneath the woes. Nearness to the light is not the same thing as walking in it, and it never was. The most exposed can become the most hardened, precisely because sustained familiarity breeds the deadliest form of indifference there is: the shrug of people who have heard it all before and stopped being moved.

### II. Hidden From the Wise, Given to the Weary — and the Sin That Cannot Be Forgiven (Matthew 11:25–12:37)

In the middle of all this rejection, Jesus does something unexpected: He prays out loud, and the prayer reveals the strange, upside-down logic of the whole kingdom. "I thank You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to babes." (Matthew 11:25) The kingdom is not hidden from intelligent people as a punishment for being intelligent; it is hidden from the self-sufficient, from the ones too full of their own wisdom and their own record to receive anything as a gift they did not earn. And then, immediately, comes the invitation that has pulled the exhausted up out of the dark for two thousand years running.

- **A. The tenderest words in the Gospel.** "Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For My yoke is easy and My burden is light." (Matthew 11:28–30) It is a deliberate echo of Jeremiah — "Stand in the ways and see, and ask for the old paths, where the good way is, and walk in it; then you will find rest for your souls" (Jeremiah 6:16) — and it is offered to precisely the people the wise had written off as hopeless. The King who is at that very moment being rejected by all the strong turns His face toward the weak and the tired and calls them in. This is the direct fulfillment of Isaiah's Servant, whom Matthew quotes just a chapter later: "A bruised reed He will not break, and smoking flax He will not quench." (Isaiah 42:3) He does not step on the reed already half-broken. He does not snuff out the wick already barely smoking. He is their rest — not a program, not a technique, not one more thing to perform. Himself, gentle and lowly, offered as the resting place.
- **B. The hardness that hardens past forgiveness.** But the same two chapters show the exact opposite response and follow it to its terrifying end. When Jesus casts a demon out of a blind and mute man, and the crowds begin to wonder aloud whether this could be the Son of David, the Pharisees have a ready answer: He casts out demons "by Beelzebub, the ruler of the demons." (Matthew 12:24) They are looking directly at the undeniable work of the Spirit of God — good, liberating, plainly and obviously divine — and calling it the work of hell. And Jesus says this, gravely: "the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven men. Anyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, either in this age or in the age to come." (Matthew 12:31–32) This is not a single careless sentence anyone stumbles into by accident and then panics about. It is a settled, deliberate, willful hardening — looking full into the light and calling it darkness, over and over, until the conscience itself can no longer respond to anything. Zechariah had described the ancestors doing the very same thing: "they made their hearts like flint, refusing to hear the law" (Zechariah 7:12). The sin that cannot be forgiven is the heart that has finally, by long practice, made itself unable to repent.

### III. The Two Ways to Refuse Him — Living Well Between the Weary and the Hard

Turn it around, because Matthew 11 and 12 put every reader somewhere on a single line — either among the weary who come, or among the hardening who refuse. And the genuinely frightening part is that the hardening almost never feels, from the inside, like rebellion. It feels like caution. It feels like being reasonable, sensible, appropriately skeptical, not naive. It happens one small refusal at a time, one shrug at a time, until one ordinary day the light simply no longer moves you at all and you do not even notice the moment it stopped. I have watched it happen slowly in others, and — this is the harder confession — I have felt the beginnings of it in myself: the sermon that no longer lands on me because I have preached it too many times to be pierced by it anymore, the familiarity that dulls the blade exactly where it ought to cut deepest. Capernaum is not only a town on the shore of Galilee. It is a condition, and a pulpit is no protection against it.

- **A. Today, if you will hear His voice.** The writer of Hebrews took this exact danger and pressed it on the early church with a word that refuses to let the reader postpone the decision to some more convenient day: "Today, if you will hear His voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion." (Hebrews 3:15) Today — not tomorrow, not once things settle down. The Proverb had already sounded the same warning centuries earlier, with even less cushioning: "He who is often rebuked, and hardens his neck, will suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy." (Proverbs 29:1) The unforgivable sin is not a single unforgivable act that God, in some fit of severity, refuses to pardon. It is a heart that has, by long and patient practice, forgiven itself out of ever wanting the pardon at all — that has said "Beelzebub" to the Spirit's plain work so many times that it can no longer form the word "come." The mercy of God is never the thing that gets withdrawn. What wears away, from the inside, one refusal at a time, is the capacity to reach out and receive it.
- **B. The gentleness that shames the strong.** And here is where these two dark chapters finally resolve — not into cheap relief, but into a door still standing open. Paul, writing to the proud and clever church at Corinth, put the same upside-down logic Jesus prayed on the mountain into a single sentence: God "has chosen the foolish things of the world to put to shame the wise, and God has chosen the weak things of the world to put to shame the things which are mighty." (1 Corinthians 1:27) The kingdom is hidden from the confident and handed to the exhausted for one reason: only the exhausted have hands empty enough to take it. The wise and prudent of Chorazin looked at the miracles and walked on by, too full to be hungry. The weary and heavy-laden came, and found rest for their souls. The King who was rejected by everyone strong enough and clever enough to reject Him is, at this very moment, still gentle and lowly in heart, still saying the same word He said in Galilee — come. To the tired. To the ashamed. To the ones utterly convinced they are too far gone to bother. The only people in the end who miss it are the ones too full to be poor, too sure to be weary, too hardened by long familiarity to hear the voice while it is still, mercifully, called today.

The invitation and the warning stand side by side in the same two chapters, and you are somewhere on the line between them right now. One heart hears "come" and comes, empty-handed and tired and welcomed. The other hears the very same word and hardens one more degree, one more shrug into the flint. The mercy is entirely real, and it is offered now, today — and it will not wait forever on a heart that is quietly, and without ever meaning to, teaching itself to stop wanting it.

Come, all who are weary.

## The Kingdom That Grows Where You Cannot See It: Matthew 13
*Why the reign of God arrives hidden, contested, and slow — and why that is the design, not the failure*

**Text:** Matthew 13 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 6:9–10 · Mark 4:26–29 · 1 Corinthians 1:27–28 · Romans 2:4–5 · Philippians 1:6 · 1 Corinthians 4:5

You were sold a kingdom that would be obvious. Somewhere in the machinery of American religion, the promise got rewired — the gospel was going to win the way a campaign wins, the way a stadium fills, the way a movement trends. And when it did not, when the numbers slid and the culture turned and the church you gave your life to grew quieter instead of louder, you began to suspect the whole thing had failed. That suspicion is not new. It sat in the crowd on the shore of Galilee, watching a carpenter tell farming stories while Rome held the roads and the temple held the coin and nothing, from the outside, looked like a throne being established. The people who wanted a Messiah wanted armies and thrones and an unmistakable end to their humiliation. What they got was a man in a boat, talking about dirt. Matthew 13 is Jesus answering that exact disappointment. He does not answer it with a program. He does not answer it with a five-year plan or a projection of growth. He answers it with seven parables about a kingdom you were never meant to see coming, and every one of them tells the same hard truth from a different angle: the reign of God is real, and it is hidden, and the hiddenness is not the failure. It is the design.

### I. The Sower and the Secret of a Kingdom Given Only to Some (Matthew 13:1–23)

He begins with the ground. A sower goes out, and the seed falls on a path, on rock, among thorns, and on good soil, and only the last one bears. It is a picture every listener knew in their hands — the failure rate of first-century farming was brutal, and no one hearing this expected every seed to grow. That is the first thing we miss. Jesus is not describing an efficient enterprise. He is describing a scattering in which most of what is sown appears to come to nothing, and he is telling a crowd hungry for guaranteed victory that the kingdom does not work the way they demanded.

The disciples ask why he teaches this way, and the answer is the hinge of the entire chapter. "To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given" (Matthew 13:11). The Greek is *mysteria* — not a puzzle to be solved by the clever, but a reality disclosed by God to whom he wills. A mystery in the biblical sense is not a riddle you crack with enough intelligence. It is something hidden that stays hidden until God opens it. The kingdom is not withheld from the sharp and handed to the dull. It is hidden from the self-sufficient and opened to the poor.

Then Jesus reaches back seven centuries and puts Isaiah in the crowd's mouth. "You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive. For this people's heart has grown dull" (Matthew 13:14–15, quoting Isaiah 6:9–10). This is the hardest thing in the chapter, and preachers hurry past it, because it will not fit our machinery of technique. The parables are not simplifications. They are not Jesus meeting the crowd where they are. They are a sieve. They reveal to the hungry and conceal from the comfortable, and the concealing is not an accident of method — it is judgment already at work in the way the word is heard. The same story that opens one heart hardens another, and the hardening is not a bug in the teaching. It is the teaching doing exactly what the prophet said it would.

- **A. The soils are not four kinds of people you meet. They are four conditions your own heart has been in.** I have preached the seed and watched it die in me — snatched away before Monday, scorched by the first real cost, choked by the very ministry that was supposed to make it grow. The path, the rock, the thorns: I have been all three, and called it faithfulness the whole time. It is far too convenient to hear this parable and start sorting the people in the pews into categories. Jesus told it to make you examine the ground under your own feet.
- **B. Fruit, not enthusiasm, is the evidence.** The good soil is defined by one thing — it "bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty" (Matthew 13:23). Not the soil that felt the most. Not the soil that responded fastest — the rocky ground did that, "immediately received it with joy" (Matthew 13:20), and it was the first to die. The soil that produced. The kingdom does not measure the height of the initial response. It measures the harvest, and the harvest comes slow, and it comes late, and it comes only where the word went deep enough to survive the drought.

### II. Weeds, Mustard, Leaven, and a Reign That Refuses to Announce Itself (Matthew 13:24–43)

The next parables answer the question underneath the shore's disappointment: if this is the kingdom, why does evil still stand in the middle of it? Why, if the King has come, does the world look untouched? A man sows good seed, and an enemy sows weeds among the wheat while everyone sleeps, and the servants — zealous, well-meaning, exactly like us — want to tear the weeds out now. The master says no — "lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. Let both grow together until the harvest" (Matthew 13:29–30). The sorting is real. It is also not yours, and it is not yet. Every generation of the church that has appointed itself the reaper has torn up wheat and called it purity. The weeds Jesus names — *zizania*, a darnel that looks almost identical to wheat until the heads form — cannot even be reliably told apart by the servants who want to pull them. The confidence with which we sort is exactly the confidence Jesus forbids.

Then the mustard seed, "the smallest of all seeds," becoming a tree where the birds nest (Matthew 13:31–32). Then the leaven a woman hides in the flour until it works all the way through (Matthew 13:33). Both are pictures of disproportion — a beginning so small it is embarrassing, an ending so large it is absurd, and no visible drama in between.
